utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: But could I deal first with her two concerns and say that the only case in the paragraphs that she has referred to that I will be placing any direct reliance upon is the decision of Lord Denning in the case at paragraph 38. And the only matters that -- from that case that she need concern her with are set out in that paragraph. So there will be no need for her to -- to read any cases. So far as the witness statements are concerned, as I understand her draft -- and I doubt that this is has changed -- she does -- the Prosecution does accept the principles of which they speak, and so it should not be necessary to go in -- into those statements in any detail or deliver any controversial matters. I think the statements are helpful as explaining from a professional perspective why journalists feel this way and why a rule adopted by this Court of more or less automatically summonsing them would put them in danger and more importantly put their sources in danger. The most important of the statements in the -- what might be termed the evidential material is the very careful and important analysis offered by Judge Richard Goldstone, the very first Prosecutor who has clearly thought through this matter a lot. And I doubt that Judge Goldstone would be the person that Ms. Korner would wish to subpoena and cross-examine. But it is his statement of principle upon which we place great reliance and seek that the Prosecutor now follow the principles that he laid down extra carefully. Can I begin, Your Honours, by inviting attention to the juristic nature of the application, which is put on two bases. What we seek to achieve is the recognition by this Court of what I would term a "public interest privilege." The word "privilege" always raises hackels particularly outside the narrow domain of lawyers who is know that it doesn't mean what it does in some languages. So let me say at once that this is a public interest qualified privilege in which we invite the courts not to hold that journalists have an immunity from testifying but that they have a presumptive right not to be forced to testify if they are unwilling except in a number of situations, which we will invite the Court to define. As Ms. Korner notes in her, at least, draft submissions, this is the first time that this Tribunal has faced what is as Your Honour has noted is not uncommon in domestic courts and has been addressed by the European court of human right, namely the position of the journalist as witness, a position that is dealt with in domestic laws alongside the position of the lawyer, the social worker, the clergyman, people who have a special relationship with the case and where it may not be appropriate for public interest reasons to compel them to testify. And it is the public interest which we rely upon as the foundation of the privilege. Another way of putting it is to say that we are asking the Court to apply a presumption -- a presumption applied through or from its own inherent power to regulate its proceedings; a presumption that journalists will not be compelled to give evidence as to their work in war zones or conflict zones, perhaps more appropriately, unless certain conditions are made out. And it may be that that way of putting it is more appropriate. That would be a matter for the Court to decide. But the basis upon which we seek either the public interest privilege or alternatively the presumption to be acknowledged in the common law of the court is related to and only related to the journalist's work in the conflict zone. Obviously information that is relevant, that is acquired by the journalist in any other capacity should be a situation dealt with according to the rules for ordinary testimony. But it is the conflict zone material that the journalist collects that is the key to this application. The reasons for it -- and I gather that there is -- these are not substantially dissented from -- as set out in our application as paragraph 11. I have -- at paragraph 11. The earlier paragraphs are simply setting, as it were, the scene in this case. Mr. Randal, whom I represent, is in fact an elderly retired journalist who worked for the Washington Post and who wrote, as Your Honours know, an article in -- way back in 1993 which contained an interview with one of the defendants. Just to summarise the facts very briefly, that interview was given by the defendant to two journalists, one of whom -- who we shall call Mr. X, spoke fluent Serbo-Croat. He'd been a Fullbright scholar in Belgrade; and Mr. Randal who spoke no Serbo-Croat relied on Mr. X for his translation, so that your -- this Court has the article that he wrote and this Court has a copy of a witness statement that Mr. Randal gave willingly when he was contacted by the office of the Prosecution which makes clear that he cannot give other than hearsay evidence, so to speak, of the conversation he had with the defendant. He can, of course, speak as to the defendant's demeanour in the course of that interview. He can, of course, speak as to Mr. X's reputation as a fluent Serbo-Croat speaker. And so one would not say - and I do not contend - that he can give no evidence at all to this Court. Those two matters may be of some interest to the Court. I shall invite at the end of the day the Court to say the amount of relevance they add to what the Court has already in the article and in the witness statement are insignificant and certainly not sufficient under the rule for which I contend to compel this journalist to testify. The other matter that Mr. Randal deals with in his witness statement which may be particularly germane to the public interest as purely as example of it is that he says that after his article was published, he was shunned and avoided by the defendant. And that, of course, goes or is an example of what we say will happen if journalists are routinely compellable to give evidence against those whom they interview, those who give them facilities in war zones to observe what may very well be war crimes. If they are routinely compellable, then they will not be given in future conflicts or in the same conflict which may, as this did, continue for some years. They will not be given interviews, they will not be afforded facilities, they will be not allowed to enter zones where they may observe war crimes. And in short, the amount of information that they are able to produce will tend to dry up. And I use that language because that was the language of the European Court of human rights when it accepted that journalists in local situations had a privilege against being forced to testify in circumstances which might expose sources. I make plain that on the facts of this case there is no confidential source involved. However, when journalists are compelled to testify to what they have seen in war zones, it may well happen that their confidential sources are exposed by way of cross-examination, by way of giving the Defence access to their notebooks. And so the confidential source issue, while it is not a primary issue in the -- on the facts of this case, is nonetheless -- must be kept in mind as one of the many dangers, one of the many matters that are contrary to the public interest that may arise if journalists are routinely required to testify. At paragraph 11, we say, having noted that the subpoena power is not absolute, we say: "It must be tailored to the recognised public interest privileges. We've recognised a public interest privilege specifically for lawyers, court employees. And there is of course in the Simic case the judgement that gives a very firm public interest privilege to Red Cross workers. We say, building upon that jurisprudence, that a Red Cross worker today, a Christian aid worker the next day or a Care worker or any indeed NGO worker would be given the advantage -- or would be given under the Red Cross rule, would be given a presumption against being compelled to testify where that public interest were at stake. We say that there is another category, namely the category of journalist, who should be entitled to, we put it, a strong presumption against requiring journalists to testify pursuant to compulsory process, a presumption that can be overcome only if the Prosecutor satisfied a test that responds to and balances the underlying policy considerations, including on the one hand in a sense the need of justice to have the journalist testimony and, on the other, the public interest in not having journalists compelled, because they will tend to dry up the amount of information the public gets about conflicts and may in certain cases put journalists' lives at risks and perhaps those of their sources. But the balancing test that we cite, which is perhaps appropriate for the Court to look at, is in the judgement of Judge Hunt in the Court of Appeal in Simic. The overriding principle, of course, of the customary international law on which we draw is provided by Article 19 of the universal declaration, the right of freedom of communication. And we shall again be relying on the Goodwin case in the -- which was brought under Article 10 of the European convention to show that that is not just a direct right of the press to report to the public; it also covers what the European Court in masses of jurisprudence now calls the watchdog role of the press, the journalist as watchdog to bark against crime and other damaging facts. What we say is that one can extrapolate from those almost universal human rights treaties requiring courts to take into account the right of freedom of expression, that the watchdog role of the journalist is particularly important and needs particular protection when the journalist is covering war and conflict, because in that situation there have lamentably -- and Your Honours will see it in the material -- there have been hundreds of deaths of journalists. Some 700 journalists have been killed in conflict zones over the past ten years. And for many -- many a week -- at the end of last year in Afghanistan, there had been more deaths of journalists than deaths of certainly US soldiers. So it is a matter that is of real concern and it is a privilege on our part to invite the Tribunal to make the first ruling on this difficult subject but important subject, drawing upon the universal -- jus cogens principle as it has been applied to journalists in other situations. Now, at 12 we set out the public interest upon which we rely. We say that "media coverage in combat zones serves firstly to provide public information -- important information to the world about international conflicts and to alert the world to the commission of war crimes." Now, that is confirmed most emphatically by Judge Goldstone, and I gather the Prosecution do not dispute it as a -- as a fact. And secondly, that journalists in their work "Provide evidential material for prosecutorial investigation, which if followed up can lead to the arrest of war criminals." So there is no sense in the which the rule for which we're contending will freeze the press out of the Prosecution process. The journalists play, as everyone knows, a significant part not only in putting information into the public domain, which many years later is followed up by prosecutors. Frequently journalists talk off the record to prosecutors and indeed to defenders. It is not as if their -- it's rather like telephone tap information in some jurisdictions which -- which is never allowed in court but which is permitted to assist prosecution investigations. There is no -- this is not a submission which excludes journalistic material from either prosecution or defence. The basis of it is that of course the work of the journalists may be relied upon and followed up by -- in mercurial process but it cannot take the form other than in exceptional cases of compelling a reluctant journalist to testify. The second principle which I think, too, the Prosecution will agree on is that these outstanding benefits for international criminal justice and Judge Goldstone makes clear that this Tribunal would not be in existence were it not for press reporting and CNN coverage and the like of the conflict in former Yugoslavia -- that these outstanding benefits for international criminal justice will only accrue if journalists are allowed to enter war zones and conduct interviews with officials in political or command responsibility positions. One could go further. They only accrue to the extent that journalists are able to inveigle their way into military operations, into places from which they may observe what's going on, as well as interviewing persons who are in command. So that's -- those two principles I think we will have significant agreement on. Thirdly -- and here the controversy, I think, begins -- if journalists are routinely compelled to give evidence subsequently to international criminal courts against those they've been permitted to observe or to interview, we say it follows logically that they will have fewer opportunities in the future. And that is because they will in the particular conflict or by the particular parties waging that conflict be regarded with suspicion, be either excluded from it or perhaps in danger if they manage to get into it. At any event, their opportunities to observe what is going on -- and the journalist provides not only, let us -- in the case of actual war crimes -- but the presence of any official observer and the presence of the journalist is a great deterrent to the commission of war crimes. It's obvious that the armies and the -- the warring parties are going to be much more careful as to how they deal with civilians if there are journalists present observing them than if they can act without any kind of observation. So whether or not the Prosecution agrees with us on 3, we say it's a pretty obvious fact of life. The fourth point is that "Routine compellability will put journalists on the whole as a collective profession at risk of greater harm and danger in conflict zones." We don't stress that point. It is because this application is not made on the basis that journalists are afraid to go into war zones. Journalists have to be, as the statements attest, particularly brave and particularly -- sometimes very devious to get into war zones. But that's their duty, and that's a duty that they will continue to do -- to conduct. But nonetheless, if it were to be the case that a Court -- and of course from July the 1st, we will have the international criminal court. And Your Honours's judgement in this case will be an important precedent for that court, which may cover dependent upon the security council and parties and so on, but which may cover conflicts anywhere in the world. But where an ad hoc court like this one has been set up in respect to a particular conflict which is ongoing, then the routine -- if that conflict goes on for eight years and if in year three or four the Court starts to compel journalists to testify about -- about what they interviewed and observed in year one, then one can well envisage that in year five the role of the journalist or the position of the journalist caught up by one of the parties that he's testified against will be very uncomfortable and very dangerous. It may be that the journalists will simply be kept out of the war zone and that that will, as I say, come in under 3 in terms of drying up information. It may be -- and one postulates possibilities here, but any death is to be avoided if possible by court rules. It may be that they would be in physical danger. Certainly if arrested, those they've been speaking to would be in great danger -- at least greater harm and danger, as we say in conflict zones. And we draw from those four propositions the fifth, that as a result routine compellability would therefore mean that less valuable information would be obtained and communicated by conflict zone reporters, including specifically information about possible or prima facie war crimes and crimes against humanity. So in order to avoid that adverse consequence, we contend that international criminal courts like this one must allow journalists a public interest privilege, a public interest and qualified privilege not to testify, or as we put it, alternatively, apply a presumption when a -- when a subpoena is sought by either the Prosecution or the Defence that the journalists should not be forced to testify. Now, can I say at once that the first point to make is that many journalists will volunteer testimony. One is not formulating a rule that will bind all journalistic consciences. There have been already in the cases heard by this Court some evidence from several journalists who have voluntarily testified. So let's -- we are not, as in the Red Cross situation, saying that no journalist should ever testify. There will be journalists who as a matter of their own conscience will feel duty-bound to testify voluntarily without a subpoena. So they -- that is their right, and no one -- least of all Mr. Randal -- would seek in any way to affect that. But the -- the first situation we come to at 13(1) is where a journalist says, "All right. I have decided that I will testify but for -- I want to do so under subpoena." Now, in that situation, when the journalist indicates clearly to the Court or to the Prosecution that he will waive the privilege, if it's a privilege, or not insist on the presumption, if it's a presumption, but he wishes to do so under subpoena, then obviously in that situation there can be no difficulty about the Court issuing the subpoena if the journalist evidence is relevant and sought by one side or the other. But the crucial part of our submissions is at 13(2), where we attempt to formulate a test. And we offer it to the Court merely as a draft, because Your Honours will -- as Your Honour has said in local law will have accounted this and will be no doubt concerned to formulate the test in different ways. But it is the key passage, "Where the Court is satisfied that the unwilling journalist, if forced to testify, will provide admissible evidence that has, we say, four characteristics. Then in that case the privilege should be overridden. The presumption is rebutted. Firstly, when the journalist -- if the evidence that the journalist can give is "Of crucial importance to its determination of a defendant's guilt or innocence." There are different ways of putting that. "Crucial importance" is simply a phrase that no doubt Your Honours can improve upon. You'll see in the cases that there are different ways of indicating that the evidence must be of very great importance either to proving the defendant guilty or to establishing the defendant's innocence. I use that terminology because the -- the more accurate one of, I suppose, raising a realistic doubt about the defendant's guilt is more appropriate where the test of guilt is beyond a reasonable doubt. But there it is. In some appropriate formulation, the first hurdle that the Prosecution must surmount when it seeks a subpoena is to establish to the Court's satisfaction that the evidence they seek from the journalist is of crucial importance, evidential importance to its case. Secondly, they have to establish -- and as I say, that is not this case, because the little tidbits of material that Mr. Randal could add -- ask they're there in his statement anyway -- are not of great significance. The second matter -- and of course it's the Court that must assess that significance. I suppose every Prosecutor thinks as every Defence counsel thinks that the evidence they want to get in is of great importance. But very how often it isn't and the Court must do that assessment for itself. The second test is -- and this is found in, I think, certainly the English and American laws on the subject -- the Court has to be satisfied that the particular evidence can't be obtained by any other means or from any other witness. And that really requires the -- the party that is seeking the subpoena to establish that it can't get the evidence any other way. Here too on the facts of this particular case, the Prosecution fail fairly dismally because they've got the evidence in the hearsay form and the journalist statement, but in any event, Mr. X, the journalist whom they don't seek to subpoena, is the person who can, one would think, give the direct evidence of what the defendant said. But it's the principle that matters rather more perhaps than the facts of this case. And that principle that you can only force a journalist to testify if you can't get the evidence in from any other means is an important and common one. C, "That the giving of this evidence by the journalist will not require him to breach any obligation of confidence." Now, that perhaps is inappropriate here because that is perhaps better under a separate rule that follows from Goodwin. But nonetheless it reflects the case law of the European Court and Goodwin in particular that where there is a confidential obligation at stake, the Court should not force the journalist to breach that. But it may, as I say, be better expressed as a separate rule. And fourthly, D, "That the giving of this evidence will not put him, or his family or his sources in any reasonably apprehended personal danger and will not unnecessarily jeopardise the effectiveness or safety of other journalists reporting from conflict zones in the future." That is a matter that must be assessed in the particular case. It may be difficult here for a journalist who's retired from the fray in respect to a journalist who wants to go back to a continuing war that is subject to the Court's jurisdiction. But in principle, again, it is important to have -- if we are formulating this rule for non-confidential cases, a third principle, that there be -- even if the evidence is highly relevant or crucial, that the compellability shouldn't -- the journalist should not be compelled to give it if there is a reasonably apprehended personal danger to himself or to his family or sources. So that -- we go on to say that that is basically our submission, that that is the formula or a formula akin to it that should be adopted either by way of a public interest privilege against testifying or by way of a presumption against testifying. And so the legal basis for the submission is set out. But I wonder if I could take you firstly to the Goldstone statement and the material just to summarise it. I don't know -- I think you have it too. And it's important, because the Washington Post is a newspaper that is -- has been celebrated over the years for its exposure of wrongdoing. I think its -- its publisher, Mr. Bo Jones, says at tab 2 sets out the basis upon which the Post supports its former journalists and its statement of policy, and this is an example of a position -- it may not be identical -- but Your Honours can expect that celebrated and significant news organisations would take in respect of this matter. And it's the third paragraph in tab 2: "The Washington Post has long maintained a policy that our reporters should not testify --"

utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robertson, sorry to interrupt you. But I've had a request to slow down because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: This is in the third paragraph at tab 2, where the publisher -- this is a statement of policy from the publisher who says: "We fully appreciate the importance of this Tribunal and in particular this trial. We recognise the need to gather evidence in order to prosecute alleged war criminals. Newspaper employees in the United States generally testify in legal proceedings like anyone else but not about their news gathering. Testimony about news gathering is different and does not serve the public interest in the long term." He goes on to explain why "Subpoenas to reporters threaten the free flow of information and compromise their ability to report the news. Compulsory process threatens our ability to cover as broadly as possible controversial public interest. They oppose subpoenas not because they believe the press is entitled to special privileges but because coerced testimony of reporters impairs the news gathering function, which is so important to democracy. And these concerns are particularly appropriate in the context of war zone reporting, war correspondents who take the witness stand risk being perceived by potential sources as an investigative arm of a judicial system, government or private parties. That perceived lack of independence threatens a journalist's ability to obtain information about conflicts. It is questionable whether the defendant in this case --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Sorry. "In 1993 if he knew that one or both of them would testify against him." And stepping -- dealing with that point for a moment, the Prosecution in its reply argues that this application has nothing to do with confidential sources. But just imagine what those sources might think if they have risked their life to tell a journalist what is happening in a conflict zone, as indeed one or two members of the SS risked their life to tell Catholic priests and journalists what was really happening in the concentration camps. If they see at this court -- or at a international court that very journalist on whose confidentiality their lives depend up in the witness box forced to testify about what he was doing in the country at about the time they spoke to him, just imagine the apprehension of those sources. Just imagine their anxiety for their own lives in that situation where the man they've entrusted that life with to give vital information -- indeed the woman -- is having their notebooks rifled by Defence counsel - quite properly - is answering questions for days on end about what they're doing and who they were seeing. That is a situation to be avoided we say not at all costs but unless the cost is the conviction of the innocent or the acquittal of the guilty. And confidential sources while they are not the subject of this application are nonetheless part -- their protection is part of the public interest reason we make it. Then Mr. Jones goes on to point out in the penultimate paragraph that "If Washington Post reporters become identified as would-be witnesses, their personal safety could be compromised and the deaths of journalists killed in conflict zones have been attributed in many cases to government or armed paramilitary objections to their work." So that is the statement from the publisher that journalist organisations feel strongly about the matter is clear from -- at tab 3 and the statement from the international federation of journalists. And the last paragraph on that page puts it in a nutshell. Two lines from the bottom "The possibility of such intimidation is greatly increased if it becomes the practice to subpoena journalists to give testimony to what they see in the course of their work. And their situation becomes ever more dangerous if their independent observer status, similar to that of humanitarian workers, Red Cross workers, and medical staff, becomes compromised." And I shall show the Court in due course the Geneva Conventions which way back in 1949 offered some protection to the journalist in combat zones by ensuring that his or her neutrality should be respected by the warring parties. So that is the position of journalist organisations. The -- at tab 4, Your Honours will find the statement of Mr. Phillip Knightley, who is one of the greatest living investigative journalists and is well known for writing the classic book about the war correspondent, by no means uncritical book, as you see from its title "The first casualty. The war correspondent as hero, propagandist, and myth maker, from the -- it should be from the Crimea to Kosovo." And so Mr. Knightley is by no means concerned to pat his own profession on the back. But at paragraph 6 he makes the point about "War correspondents having to endure the hostility of just about everyone else in the battle zone. The military, even one zone, consider the media a menace and would dearly love to get on with winning the war without having war correspondents looking over their shoulder." And so he talks about the enormous responsibility of the war correspondent. And at paragraph 10, he says: "In order to function, such a correspondent has to be seen by all parties as objective and independent ad hoc to no one, thoroughly trustworthy and determined to publish the truth. For such a person to be called later as a witness in a war crimes trial would mean that no one would ever again agree to be interviewed by them; their sources would dry up; in effect, their career as a war correspondent would be over. And then the danger of having them deceived as playing a double game." And then at 13, he refers to the Red Cross seminar on the war correspondent and the dangers of making them compellable. And at 14, "It is my considered opinion that any journalist who is later a witness at a war crimes trial could be considered by a participant or source to have been masquerading as a journalist when his real role was to gather evidence of war crimes. Journalists to do their job properly must have that independence and must not act or be seen as acting as an arm of the Prosecution. They are not policemen. They are journalists." And then at 5, we have Mr. Gutman's statement. He is a correspondent who's published a guide for journalists in covering war zones, which guide had an introduction by Richard Goldstone, who of course was the judge who was the first chief prosecutor. And if I can take you to his -- Judge Goldstone's view of this issue is to be found at tab 6 in his forward to Mr. Gutman's book. And this is a book that, as I say, is for journalists and others to educate them about crimes against humanity and the importance of courts like this. And if I could -- the second paragraph -- the second paragraph on the first page, just below the paragraph in heavy type, he writes: "Perhaps the most dramatic recent example of the impact of war reporting is the establishment of this Tribunal. Visual and written reports of the plight of the victims of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia" -- and Mr. Randal's report in this case and others is one of them -- "jolted the security council into taking the unprecedented step of creating the court." And the last sentence in that paragraph: "There can be no doubt it was media exposure that triggered the decision." And then in the next paragraph, he admits that in his first year of office he spent a substantial part of his time briefing journalists to explain the importance of the court. Then over the page, the first paragraph at the top: "The International Community is on its way to creating a court which has now been created. It's time to ask what lessons have been learnt." He talks about the difficult challenge of conflict reporting, the lack of public understanding of humanitarian law. But he adds this: "The relationship between war correspondents and the international courts has already created a tension." And here we are to see if that tension can be dissipated by an appropriate rule formulation. "As international tribunals are established," he go goes on, "journalism has gained a new and as yet undefined dimension. Journalists have very different mandates, et cetera. The two functions should not be confused." And he says this, which you may think is really a restatement of Mr. Knightley's statement: "It is important that reporters stay reporters, that is, uncover and write the story and the story behind the story for the general public." And then over the page at the very top, he talks about the -- the need, having talked about the dangers of journalists, the risks they take upon themselves. Four lines from the top of the last page: "Hence, there's an even greater need for measures to protect journalists." And then skipping over the -- he talks of the Tribunal. And then the next paragraph is the important one -- or next two are the ones upon which we rely: "Should the role of reporters extend to taking part in Tribunal prosecutions? This is not covered in the conventions nor is it likely to be. Not infrequently journalists come across evidence of war crimes as eyewitnesses in discovering a mass grave or through being privy to statements made by commanders in the heat of the action." That's this case, in a sense. "Like aid workers and Red Cross or Red Crescent delegates. If reporters become identified as would-be witnesses, their safety and future ability to be present at a field of battle will be compromised. In my opinion, the law takes too little account of that reality. And this, I would therefore, support a rule of law to protect journalists from becoming unwilling witnesses in situations that would place them or their colleagues in future jeopardy. As already indicated, the same should apply to humanitarian aid workers and Red Cross or Red Crescent delegates. That was a prescient statement in view of the decision in Simic. They should not be compelled to testify less they give up their ability to work in the field. But they may, of course, testify voluntarily." Well, if that were a court judgement, we would be relying upon it. It hits the nail right on the head. It is the rationale for this application stated powerfully but reasonably and sensibly, as one would expect, from Judge Goldstone. He does not go on to formulate the test. It may be that he's arguing for an absolute immunity. We're certainly doing nothing of that sort, but it may be that had he put his mind to it, he would have formulated a test similar to the one that we have invited. I think the -- they are the witness statements. And I don't think I need bother -- oh, at 9 you will see the Geneva Conventions protections. And of course this was back in 1949, but it was -- and there was the protocol in 1977 that "Measures for protection of journalists. Journalists engaged in dangerous professional missions should be considered as civilians provided." In 2, "They take no action adversely affecting their status but they are accredited to a particular party." Now, the significance of this is simply that under the Geneva Conventions journalists are entitled to be accredited to one side or the either in a war. They are given this neutral status as civilians -- in other words, they must be treated with the same consideration as civilians under -- protected under the Geneva Convention because they are not in fact viewed as participants or as willing members of the force to whom they're accredited unless they take action, as one or two journalists have done over the years and been condemned for doing, of -- involving themselves in one side's propaganda or even -- or taking up arms for one -- for that side. So there the Geneva Convention we say recognises through that rule the importance of protecting journalists in war situations. And that is the basis for -- or the beginning of the customary international law requirement that journalists be protected. At 11, you will note the European position on protection of sources. And this is as a result in part of Goodwin. And then at tab 12 is the recommendation on the -- to the Committee of Ministers that journalists should not be required to disclose their sources of information. And paragraph 3 refers to the Goodwin case. And at 5, six lines down, after Goodwin is referred to the same says that any disclosure of a source may have a chilling effect on the readiness of future sources to provide journalists with information. And it is in this case, we say, the chilling effect on the readiness of future commanders, leaders, generals, and politicians in positions of power to provide journalists with information. That is the public interest reason for the qualified privilege or presumption that we seek. At 13, there is another -- there is significantly the Committee of Ministers set out the need to protect journalists in situations of conflict and tension. And at 2, the appeal is made by the committee to all member states of the Council of Europe to recognise that the right of individuals and the general public to be informed about all matters of public interest is especially important in situations of conflict and tension. And at 3, they solemnly reaffirm that journalists working in such situations without qualification entitled to the full protection of such laws and treaties as apply to them, including, we would say, by full protection the way in which the treaty policy can be developed or in particular mercurial situations like this. And at -- finally, at tab 14, you will see the recommendation adopted in 1996 by the Committee of Ministers on the protection of journalists in situation of conflict, which preamble, begins, by noting the danger that journalists face and the importance of their work. On the second page -- or at the bottom of the first page and the top of the second page it notes the Geneva protocols, which I've shown to the Court, protecting journalists by having their neutral status confirmed, although they were attached to a force. Four lines down: "Convinced that it is necessary to reaffirm these guarantees to ensure they are respected with a view to strengthening the protection of journalists in situations of conflict and tension, stressing that any interference must be exceptional, be kept to a minimum, and be strictly in line with relevant human rights instruments." We rely on that passage. "Compulsory testimony is interfering with the work of journalists. So it should be exceptional and kept to a minimum. And the formulation of the rule that we suggest or any similar formulation is designed to ensure that journalists are only compelled to testify in exceptional cases." And then it recommends that the governments be guided in their actions and policies by these principles. And of course, we would invite the Court to accept that it is perhaps within that predecessor. Could I go back, if I may. I've dealt with all the appendices now -- to tab 1, to our argument, and deal very briefly with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now take Your Honours back, if I may, to our application in paragraph 15, where we make the point that the power to subpoena is not absolute. And we give examples of well-known categories of immunity. We don't suggest that the journalist's immunity is as extensive as the lawyer's immunity or the state official's immunity or indeed the Red Cross official's immunity. But it is nonetheless significant that in the analysis that was given in Simic -- and we set it out at paragraph 18 -- that what the Court was doing was in fact looking at the protection given to Red Cross workers by the Geneva Conventions and implying from that a powerful public interest privilege, so powerful indeed that in the view of the majority there could be no question but that the Red Cross and Red Crescent as organisations could compel their former employees not to testify. We find that a most absolute approach which is not echoed by Judge Hunt, who does apply the more conventional balancing test. But nonetheless again draws from the Geneva Conventions and the fact that there is a protection for the Red Cross there as there is a protection for journalists a policy, a public interest policy that we say, is present on the facts of this case. There is a public interest policy that journalists be not routinely compellable. Mr. Randal happens to be retired, but Your Honours I'm sure can envisage and know that there are many journalist who have been active in the area since the early 1990s who in this Tribunal's jurisdiction over the area is continuing, and those journalists will go back to Belgrade, to Pristina, to places in Bosnia and will face if summonsed, if they have given evidence, and this is televised and they are perceived to have given evidence against the defendant or indeed on behalf of the defendant, they will be seen as party pre. They will be -- I'm not suggesting that they will be assaulted. Although that may be the strength of feeling that exists in some places. It may put them in some physical danger. But more importantly for their work, people who sympathise with the party against whom they have been perceived as testifying will not talk to them or will act aggressively against them. And it may be that journalists compelled to testify will in effect be forced to end their work in the area. So that is the -- what we draw from the Red Cross cases. And we mention at 19 the Trial Chamber's decision refusing to subpoena an interpreter. I would imagine that that -- one can conceive of situations where an interpreter can give very relevant evidence. And one suspects that if that position were to recur, there would be a balancing operation after the -- after a presumption. But -- and then Commander-in-Chief. And we note the position at the ICC and that this case will be a precedent for it. At 23, we summarise the position that there is no absolute power in the court under Rule 54. There are clear limitations, policy limitations on the application in 54, and that one of them supports the qualification. And we set out Judge Hunt's approach in Simic as similar to the approach that we would urge. He use it is words -- I think in our formulation we had suggested that the evidence should be not only admissible but of crucial importance to the determination of guilt or innocence. Judge Hunt says at the bottom of that quote at paragraph 24 that "The test should be essential or indispensable," he suggests, as the basis for that particular test, when the balancing act is being carried out. And so we say that -- and this was, of course, overriding the Red Cross's decision not to let the employee testify when the evidence is vital to establish innocence or vital to establish guilt. And then at 25, we draw again on Judge Goldstone's foreword. And then at -- and set out the matters that I have read from him at 27. And at 28 note the Red Cross's commentary on Article 79 of the Geneva Conventions which sets out the protocols protection of journalists. At the top of page 11, the Red Cross says "The circumstances of armed conflict expose journalists exercising their profession to dangers which often exceed the level of danger normally encountered by civilians." That is important because the cases upon which the Prosecution rely are cases notably Branzburg and Hayes, in which the protection is sought in a country that is at peace where there is no civil war and it was only a protection to go in secret to the grand jury. It wasn't a protection at trial. But we'll come to that. The Red Cross says that special rules are required for journalists who were imperiled by their professional duties in the context of armed conflict. Of the -- there are only three cases that I need show the Court. The -- at paragraph 30, we refer to the -- it's a long case, and you'll find it in the bundle. It's a famous case. I think Judge Burgental [phoen] and others at the inter-American court decided that journalists should not be subject to licensing by the state. A journalist is one who exercises by occupation a right of freedom of expression which is available to all under the human rights treaties. But the -- insofar as the Prosecution case says, journalists aren't noted -- noticed by international law, international law takes no concern about journalists. That's not so. This case -- famous case quite early in the -- in 1985 established that journalists do have international law protection. The case of Goodwin, I think we have -- you will find at -- in your bundle at 9. Does -- do Your Honours have the case bundles?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: And the -- the discussion that's relevant begins at paragraph 37. And the question of whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society, one of the important facts was that the journalist -- the article that had been written by the journalist was the subject of an injunction which restrained publication of the secret. So the -- the plaintiff had achieved some measure of protection, and he wanted more by identifying the source that he suspected had stolen the secret plan. And the fact that there was some protection in place by way of the injunction against publication was important when the Court went on to consider proportionality. And we say, on the same basis, that the fact that you have -- the Court has Mr. Randal's statement and has the article is -- gives it sufficient material already. Paragraph 39 is the paragraph that we rely upon, particularly in the second -- the second paragraph of that paragraph, halfway down: "Having set out the resolutions by the Committee of Ministers, without such protection, sources may be deterred from assisting the press in informing the public on matters of public interest. As a result, the vital public watchdog role of the press may be undermined and the ability of the press to provide accurate and reliable information may be adversely affected." So that establishes the reason for the privilege is the public watchdog role of the press and the need to ensure -- to encourage information to be supplied to it. That is the same public interest that we rely upon, and it's all the more crucial, we say, in situations of war reporting. This case arose from the most specific environment of a business reporter. And so at 40, you will find the necessity for any coercive action must be convincingly established to answer to a pressing social need. At 42, the proportionality principle. The plaintiff had some measure of protection and didn't need to force the journalist to testify. And at 46, there was not a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the aim pursued by the disclosure order, and the means deployed to achieve that aim. That is the -- another example of international law giving protection to journalists, albeit in peacetime, for the public policy reasons that are even more acute in times of war. Moving on, if I may, in our argument to the section on domestic protection, we cite a number of cases from the United States. And I -- the Prosecution has said, "Well, wait a minute. The controlling case in the United States is Branzburg and Hayes, which did not give the journalist the protection of the kind that you allege. Can I make these points on Branzburg: Firstly, it was a case in 1972. The law in both countries has moved on. Secondly, it was a decision that needs to be carefully analysed. The Prosecution has quoted only from the four-judge majority. But there were four judges who held that the journalistic privilege did indeed exist. Justice Douglas, who said it was absolute, and the other judges - Brennan, Stewart and Marshall, three judges whose judgements have tended to be accepted by international human rights courts - who held that there was a qualified privilege. So it was four-all. And the crucial judgement is that short judgement in the middle of Mr. Justice Powell. If I may -- and I think that's described as elliptical. I don't know whether you -- what tab number you have Branzburg at. I think we are both using the same Internet version of it. But Justice Powell's decision, which has in fact allowed state courts and federal courts to develop journalistic qualified privilege in the States, is at page 24 of Branzburg, at -- on the right-hand side. It's described by the minority, Stewart, Brennan, and Marshall, as an enigmatic concurring opinion. They say, at paragraph 725: "Mr. Justice Powell's enigmatic concurring opinion gives hope of a flexible view in the future." And they go on to state the privilege. But the -- Mr. Justice Powell, at page 24 - it's paragraph 709 - begins by saying -- emphasising the limited nature of the Court's holding. And at 710, five lines down the second paragraph, he says: "Indeed, if the newsman is called upon to give information bearing a remote tenuous relationship to the subject of investigation or if he believes testimony implicates confidential source relationship without legitimate need of law enforcement, he will have access to the court on a motion to quash and an appropriate protective order may be entered. The asserted claim to privilege should be judged on its facts by the striking of a proper balance between freedom of the press and the obligation of citizens to give relevant testimony." So that is all that Justice Powell says. That is the swing vote on the Court. And as over the page, at 725, you will see the dissenters, who are all for a qualified privilege, say that that enigmatic concurring opinion gives hope of a more flexible view. And at paragraph 34, we set out some cases where the flexible view has been taken where the courts in America have held that the public interest is an interest of sufficient social importance to justify some incidental sacrifice of sources and facts needed in the administration of justice. And they talk about the state shield laws. And at 35, importantly, "The reporter's privilege shields not only the identity of sources but the information acquired by a reporter regardless of whether the information or the source is confidential." And that is in Shoen, which is one of the cases that we have put before the Court. And we cite that the -- the quote: "The compelled production of a reporter's resource materials can constitute a significant intrusion." And "Like the compelled disclosure of confidential sources, it may undercut the public policy favouring the free flow of information which is the foundation of the privilege." And then at 36, we say, two lines down, that as a result of the development of American law since Branzburg, the party seeking news-gathering information must show two things; first of all that disclosure must go to the heart of the matter, which is perhaps a -- an appropriate way of putting it in common terms. The crunch is whether -- crunch question is whether it goes to the heart of the matter or is crucial to his case. It's not enough that information is just relevant. Secondly, "The party seeking disclosure must demonstrate that he or she has 'exhausted every reasonable alternative source of information.'" Well, then, we say they are the formulations of A and B in our formulation and they would be perfectly acceptable. That seems to be the -- the point to which American law has reached. At 37, we note the Justice Department guidelines in America create a presumption against subpoenaing members of the news media. They've got to get the approval of the attorney general; they've got to balance the First Amendment interest with law enforcement; they've got to take all reasonable attempts to get the information from other sources; it's got to be essential, and so on. And I think we have put the -- I think you have -- or should have somewhere - and could I just check - a document called the Code of Federal Regulations, title 28, Department of Justice Policy. And we've extracted from that the policy with regard to the issuance of subpoenas to members of the news media. Do Your Honours have that? If not, we will hand up copies.
