utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: We haven't extracted the Tribunal cases. The cases begin at 7 with the Sener and Turkey. Then there is, at 8, there's the inter-American case I mentioned. Then at 9, Goodwin, which you have looked at in the Prosecution bundle. Then 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 are American cases. Tab 16 is the Internal Guidelines of the Department of justice, which I have -- which perhaps I can just show you is the policy with regard to the issuance of subpoenas. And that's the policy that I've described. This is the document that the department of justice issues to its prosecutors and the guidelines that must be adhered to. And you see guideline A in determining whether to request issuance of a subpoena, the approach must be to strike the proper balance between the public interest in ideas and information and in effective law enforcement; B, all reasonable steps to go to alternative sources; C, negotiate with the media before issuing a subpoena and so forth. E is you've got to get the express approval of the attorney general. And then at F(1), the attorney general's authorisation will only be given in certain circumstances. The information sought must be essential with reference directly to establishing guilt or innocence. The subpoena should not be used for non-essential information. And 3 is the -- try and get it from other sources. 4, the use of subpoenas should be limited to verification of published information, and so forth. So that shows what the position really is, and it does put into perspective the claims that the Prosecution make on the basis of Branzburg and Hayes, an inaccurate reading of it of a case that has long been superseded by the cases that we have presented and the code for federal prosecutors. The position in England we set out at paragraph 38. And you will find the judgement in Senior v. Holdsworth at tab 17, just after the code for federal prosecutors. That was a case which was argued interestingly enough by Gordon Slynn, who became at page 27 -- who played various important parts in European positions before going to the House of Lords, where he sits today. Lord Denning set out -- whose judgement begins at page 30 -- explains the facts and the subpoena. And the passages that we rely upon are at page 34 and 35. And at the bottom where he concludes that the Court has power to issue the subpoena for the untransmitted film, the Court should -- in the last line "Only exercise this power when the film has a direct and important place in the evidence." And so we can go back, in fact, to the -- to paragraph 38, where Lord Denning's words about the "Special position of the journalist who gathers news of public concern. The courts respect his work and will not hamper it more than necessary." And he talks about the public interest in seeing that confidences are respected and that newsmen are not hampered by fear of being compelled to disclose all the information which comes their way. So "The judge will not direct the newsperson to answer unless it is not only relevant but it is a proper and necessary question to be put." So there is the Lord Denning putting the test as a presumption in a non-confidential case. The case arose from news film which had been shot at a pop festival of a disturbance and the Court refused to allow the party to subpoena the photographers to show the film. There was nothing confidential about them but the public interest was against the compulsion. And then the case of Bright is the next case. We deal with it at paragraph 39. It involved a member of the British security service who had spoken to the press and sought political asylum, which he was actually given by the French courts in Paris, and had accused the British secret service of seeking to assassinate Colonel Kadafi. And there was no confidentiality again involved. The police -- his letter again that he had written to the newspaper and the newspaper inquiries about him. But even in national security case safeguards were imposed on -- for the press and the Court held that because there was a public interest at stake, compelling evidence was needed by the police to demonstrate that the subpoena would override that public interest. So at 41 we state our preliminary conclusion on the case law in the way that I've identified. And I needn't perhaps read it. It really sums up what I've been advocating to the Court. The theme in the case law -- the fact that protection does exist for journalists in international law -- it has since the Geneva Convention, since the inter-American court, since the European Court. It's a protection based on public interest in the watchdog role. It is crucial, most important in war zone reporting. And this Court can put that protection into Tribunal law in -- either by granting a public interest privilege qualified in the way that we've suggested or by creating from its inherent power a presumption against issuing compulsory process against journalists except in those extraordinary situations. That is the principle and that is what I wish to really address you on. There are some specific considerations in relation to Mr. Randal and when -- when the Court comes to apply whatever it considers to be the right principle to the fact of Mr. Randal's case. We simply note that the -- it could not be said that this evidence is vital to convict the defendant. It is strictly hearsay. Mr. Randal cannot in the circumstances, because he doesn't know the language, give evidence to the Court confirming that those were the precise words said by the defendant. And so Mr. Randal is not a voluntary witness. He does not wish to give evidence. He wishes to assert the privilege which we have argued that he has or alternatively have the benefit of the presumption against testifying. This is not a case that meets the requirements however they are formulated in -- in either of a privilege or of a presumption. And Your Honours, thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Robertson, before you sit down, I've noticed that you have omitted completely any reference to the Rules and practice of this Tribunal as they relate to protective measures that are extended to sensitive witnesses, in particular -- particularly witnesses that may be exposed to physical danger, personal danger, if details to their particulars or even details as to the fact that they have given evidence in this Tribunal is made public. Do you think that a reference to these provisions is relevant to your argument or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: We did consider whether -- the relevance. And we're very grateful to Your Honour for pointing out that it could have relevance. But we were inclined to think that the principle for which we contend would not be satisfactorily dealt with by protective measures, because firstly, the journalist -- protective measures may be appropriate if the journalist willingly testifies but says, "I want to do it in private or I want to do it without my address being given or without my name being given." A journalist who willingly testifies could ask and -- and maybe in a situation of asking for protective measures. But we do not think -- and certainly this case doesn't raise the issue of protective measures. We do not think that compelling a journalist to testify but giving him, for example, anonymity or a closed hearing would really be appropriate. Journalists who would not wish themselves to be perceived as participating in a closed hearing, because all sorts of rumours would get around as to what they were saying. Either the Prosecution or the Defence out of court could set those rumours off, or it may be that they would arise anyway. Here is a man to whom you have, if you're a source, entrusted perhaps your life. Here is a man who has to go back to a conflict zone, and he's going into this secret court giving evidence for the Prosecution -- that much would probably get known. It would be -- it would be inappropriate, we say, to compel him but give him the benefit of such measures which may seal his fate or seal the fate of his informants far more readily than any evidence that he were actually to give. In any event, we suspect that attempting to cover up the name of -- the name of the journalist, which of course is not this case. Mr. Randal is -- is known to the defendant. But attempting to cover up the name of the journalist would be equally problematic because certainly security organisations, states parties would know in all probability who he was. So for that reason, while we could take advantage, I suppose, of the fact that protective measures exist, the -- it would be inappropriate, we say, to compel the journalist with the offer of protective measures. And of course, it's not just a position with one journalist. We say that routine compellability does put future journalists at risk. So that's how we would deal with the question of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Robertson. Perhaps -- yes, Ms. Korner now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. May it please Your Honours. Your Honours, I think one ought to remind ourselves of how this matter has come before Your Honours in the first place, the actual facts, because certainly part of our submission is that Your Honours are being asked to make a ruling effectively of principle but we will be saying on a most unmeritorious set of facts before Your Honours. Your Honours, on February the 11th, 1993 the Washington Post published the article by Mr. Randal which is the subject of this argument. Your Honours, I don't know whether Your Honours have got that to hand, because it's worth reminding ourselves when looking at the principle of whether or not what the journalist has to say goes directly to the heart of the case is a matter which Your Honours will have to look at when exercising what we would suggest is Your Honours' discretion in the matter. Do Your Honours have that article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I hand -- although you've had it before, I did bring three more copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen it obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Might the interpreters have a copy of the article as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't. This article has been handed out on a number of occasions. I simply brought more copies for Their Honours. Your Honours, Mr. Randal conducted in writing an article about effectively the -- actually, I've got one more copy. I noticed that Her Honour Judge Janu had to give it up. I've got one more. Could Your Honours forgive me while I just look for ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, might the interpreters be given copies of the article, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While writing an article about the situation in Banja Luka in February of 1993, interviewed -- if Your Honours look at page 2 it's about -- the penultimate paragraph, what is described as Bosnian housing administrator Radoslav Brdjanin, an avowed radical Serb nationalist, who said, in quotes: "Personally argued that those unwilling to defend Serb territory must be moved out but that the Serb political leadership so far had not agreed. He said he believes the exodus of non-Serbs should be carried out peacefully so as to create an ethically clean space through voluntary movement. Muslims and Croats, he said, should not be killed but should be allowed to leave and good riddance." Now, Your Honour, that, in our submission, goes directly to the heart of this case. It is the Prosecution's contention that the reason for the crimes that we allege were carried out by Radoslav Brdjanin together with his co-accused Momir Talic and others was to rid the territory of the non-Serbian population. Now, Your Honours, there's no indication from that article as published that there was an interpreter; although, I suppose, common sense would have indicated that it was likely that Mr. Randal spoke the language. But that only became clear when he made a voluntary - and I emphasise this - a voluntary statement -- albeit with some reluctance, and we accept that -- to an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor. And it was then that it became clear that another journalist who did speak the language had been acting as an interpreter. Now, we've attached to the copies that Your Honour have the article that that journalist wrote some three days later. And it does not contain the quotes that Mr. Randal had in his article. And one of the reasons, apart from anything else, that Mr. Randal was seen and asked to make a statement was that he did in his article have those quotes. Now, Your Honour, leaving aside for the moment a matter which is touched upon, which is that we have not sought to issue a summons against the other journalist. Your Honour, I don't think that's the place to go into it, and I don't think it's really pressed I note, with any great force by Mr. Robertson in his oral argument to you. The issue is, Your Honour, is a journalist and in this particular case a journalist who has made a statement to the Prosecution compellable to testify about the matters there referred to. Now, Your Honour, there are, it seems to us, two issues: One which is a matter of general principle -- in other words, may journalists as a class of society be compelled to testify in a criminal trial, in an international criminal trial, if they can provide relevant -- and I'm using a quote from a case that I'm going to return to because it is one of the leading cases even -- although it was decided in 1963, which is the case of the Queen against Mulholland and Foster -- relevant and useful purpose to the proceedings at hand. In other words, does it go to a -- an issue which is material to the case. Your Honour, from that, one follows with this: If the answer to that is yes, and we suggest on all authority up until today the, as it were, privilege or the exemption from testifying, which the journalists themselves as you've seen from the editor's statement and the various other journalists -- that the journalists themselves would wish to have a complete blanket privilege from being compelled to testify about matters that they have witnesses -- they have witnessed - I'm sorry - or about how that information has been obtained. And for obvious reasons as we will be submitting, no court has agreed to grant them that exemption. But Your Honour, if that is right, that there cannot be a complete exemption from a compulsion to testify, then one has to go, as it were, a step further. Does it come down to this, a matter of fact and degree in each case whether the courts should enforce a compulsion by way of subpoena to testify? In other words, does it depend on the nature of the offence? Does the evidence which it appears the journalist can give go to a major issue rather than a peripheral one? And effectively, what is argued for here, that war reporter, reporters -- journalists who report from theatres of conflict should be given an exemption as a special class within the class of journalism as a whole. Your Honours, that's the first matter. And that's -- really the issue of principle that Your Honours are being asked to rule upon. The second matter is on the facts of this case, should Mr. Randal be compelled to testify on the basis of the witness statement that he made to the Prosecution? Now, Your Honours, can I go back to the first issue. Should journalists as a class of person be exempt from being compelled to testify about their sources or matters they have in fact seen or interviews that they have conducted with persons who stand accused or can give relevant evidence? Your Honour, we submit this, that in every jurisdiction that Your Honours looked at, both in the United States and in the United Kingdom -- I regret to say we haven't investigated what happens in European countries due to the limited time. But I'm sure that where there's such an exemption, it would have been raised by Mr. Robertson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's easily available. I downloaded it this morning. I haven't gone through it, but it is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, as I say, because I think we were all rather rushed on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can I say I know that -- or I'm sure that those who instruct my learned friends would have produced that if there was anything in their favour to show that. Your Honours, the principle appears to be this, that there is no privilege, there is no exemption for journalists testifying but there are certain safeguards which the courts are prepared to put into place in order to ensure as has been said over and over again the freedom of information, the role which journalists undoubtedly play in bringing to public attention crimes and other allied misdemeanours. But Your Honours, to grant them the exemption that is sought -- and it's our submission that -- even Mr. Robertson is not pursuing that one with much vigour -- namely they should never have to be compelled to testify -- were to give them a unique status not granted to any other member of the public. And journalists are no more than that. They have a job, but they are just members of the public. Your Honours, can I ask Your Honours to look first of all at the case of Mulholland and Foster, which I think Your Honours -- I don't know whether what bundle Your Honours are working off, ours or the applicants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In this particular case, I think Mulholland --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is easier to find in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm told that you got -- I'm told by Ms. Gustin you got a set.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, this -- Lord Denning, who's been referred to by Mr. Robertson in the later of Senior v. Holdsworth, to which I will return, was one of -- as Mr. Robertson says, one of the leading judges in the last century and is responsible, I think, for more or -- leading judgements and almost anything else one can think of. This was -- this case arose out of the Vassall spy saga in the early 1960s, and it was a question of whether the journalist who had published articles about Mr. Vassall and about really the lack of the British authorities to notice his spying activities could be compelled to disclose the source of the information. And Your Honour, we must emphasise as we have already in our argument on which I rely -- and I'm not going to go through it because I know Your Honours will be a chance to read it later -- that all the cases with one or two exceptions are of the question of journalists revealing their sources. There are almost none that deal with the question of a journalist who has published an article appearing to effectively confirm that that article was truthful and accurate. And it's noteworthy, Your Honour, that the Prosecution are prepared simply to put the article in to save Mr. Randal testifying and the Defence -- and that is entirely their right -- declined to agree, which we would also add shows the importance of -- of this particular article. Your Honour, with that digression, can I take, Your Honour, to what was said by Lord Denning about journalists --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must at this point interrupt in assert an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner says my objection shows the importance of the particular article. And that's not the case. My objection is as to the inaccuracy of the article, that it is an unfair representation of the conversation, and that the report by journalist acts as a fair representation of the conversation. And I suspect that the statements that Mr. Randal put in there were a result of a misunderstanding of translations from the other journalist. So I at least have a suspicion that it's inaccurate. And I'm not -- I did not object on the basis that she suggests to Your Honours, and I want to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall Mr. Ackerman making that point when we were discussing the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, apart from the fact -- I don't want to get into argument about -- because that's not the point. It doesn't detract from the point I'm making. Because if it was wholly unimportant to any issue in this case, then whether or not the quotes were accurate or inaccurate would not matter. And were it unimportant, the Prosecution wouldn't be seeking to put this article in the way that it is. Your Honour, may I now come back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Lord Denning's judgement. It's -- I should add that it's reported in the All England Law Reports (1963) at 1 All England. At the bottom of page 770, it is said -- and this is the second point -- that "However relevant the questions were and however proper to be answered for the purpose of the inquiry -- the journalist had declined to answer the questions at the inquiry -- a journalist has a privilege by law entitling him to refuse to give his source of information. The journalist puts forward as his justification the pursuit of truth. It is in the public interest, he says, that he should obtain information in confidence and publish it to the world at large, for by so doing he brings to public notice that which they should know. He can expose wrongdoing and neglective duty which would otherwise go unremedied. He cannot get this information, he says, unless he keeps the source of it secret. The mouths of his informants will be closed to him if it is known that their identity will be disclosed. So he claims to be entitled to publish all his information without ever being under any obligation even when directed by the Court or a judge to disclose whence he got it. It seems to me that the journalist put the matter much too high. The only profession that I know which is given a privilege from disclosing information to a court of law is the legal profession, and then it is not the privilege of the lawyer but of his client. Take the clergyman, the banker, or the medical man. None of these is entitled to refuse to answer when directed to by a judge. Let me not be mistaken. The judge will respect the confidences which each member of these honourable professions receives in the course of it and will not direct him to answer unless not only is it relevant but also it is a proper and indeed necessary question in the course of justice to be put and answered. A judge is the person entrusted on behalf of the community to weigh these conflicting interests, to weigh on the one hand the respect due to confidence in the profession and on the other hand the respect due to confidence --" I'm sorry -- "and on the other hand the ultimate interest of the community in justice being done, or in the case of a tribunal such as this, in a proper investigation being made into these serious allegations. If the judge determine that is the journalist must answer, then no privilege will avail him to refuse." Your Honour, they then go back to the facts. And if I can skip that -- and no doubt if there's anything Mr. Robertson wants to draw your attention to, he can do it in his reply -- and turn to the next page, 772, in the paragraph beginning: "It seems to me therefore that the authorities are all one way. There is no privilege known to the law by which a journalist can refuse to answer a question which is relevant to the inquiry and one that which in the opinion of the judge is proper for him to be asked." And Lord Denning went on to say that this was a proper case. Lord Donovan, who -- Lord Justice Donovan, I'm sorry, who was sitting with him, said this: "I agree, and added a few words about the residual discretion in a court of trial." And we would argue that that's really what it comes down to. It's a matter of discretion. "Whilst the journalist has no privilege entitling him of the right to refuse to disclose the source, so I think the interrogator has no absolute right to require such disclosure. In the first place, the question has to be relevant to be admissible at all. In the second place, it ought to be the answer to which -- and these are the words I quoted -- "will serve a useful purpose in relation to the proceedings at hand." I prefer that expression to the term "necessary." "Both these matters are for the consideration and if need be the decision of the judge. And over and above these two requirements, there may be other considerations impossible to define in advance but arising out of the infinite variety of fact and circumstance which a Court encounters which may lead a judge to conclude that more harm than good would result from compelling a disclosure or punishing a refusal to answer. For these reasons, I think that it would be wrong to hold that a judge is tied hand and foot in such a case as the present and must always order an answer or punish a refusal to give the answer once it is shown that the question is technically admissible. Indeed, I understood the learned attorney general to concur in this view, namely that the judge should always keep an ultimate discretion. This would apply not only in the case of journalists but in other cases where information is given and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I saw the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. The problem is we are not using this, therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, that is still, we would submit, the classic statement of principle. Your Honours, in the later other leading case in the United Kingdom on these matters, which is the -- it was a civil as opposed to a criminal case, which is the British Steel Corporation against Granada Television Limited which dealt with an expose so-called by Granada of British Steel. Their Lordships' service went right up to the House of Lords. And Their Lordships there quoted Mulholland the dictor in Mulholland and Foster approvingly. And with Lord Salmon dissenting -- and I'm not going to go through it Your Honours have a copy. It's very lengthy because it's reported right from the divisional court through the Court of Appeal up to the House of Lords. The appeal was dismissed, and the -- the ruling was that the media of information and journalists who wrote or contributed for them had no immunity based on public interest which protected them from an obligation to disclose in a court of law their sources of information when such a disclosure was necessary in the interest of justice. Now, Your Honour, I'll come back to the case of Senior v. Holdsworth, which was quoted. But Your Honours, can I express or distil, I hope, what we would suppose is the principles that arise. It would be wrong to give journalists a blanket exemption from ever testifying. And the reason doesn't have to go -- or doesn't have to look very far. It would give a licence to journalists to print what they liked, how they liked without any fear of ever having to justify their sources or the information that they were printing. And that is why no court in any land in our submission would ever agree to such a blanket principle. I'll come to the suggestion -- the situation as regards reporters reporting from a theatre of war in a moment, but can I just conclude what I say looking at the case of Senior v. Holdsworth, which was referred to by Mr. Robertson, decided in 1975. It's worth noting that Lord Denning was one of the last judges who was able to sit until well after the age of 80. And this in fact again was a civil action where ITN, who are one of the news organisations, it's fair to say, as Your Honours have seen who not only have been actively operating in theatres of war, as is referred to in -- I think it's Mr. -- the journalist's article statement -- I've forgotten his name now -- the man who wrote the book -- Gutman, yes, Roy Gutman -- that ITN were the first to bring to public attention the atrocities in Omarska and Trnopolje and had no hesitation at all in assisting in the Prosecution. Mr. Gutman says they suffered for it. As far as we understand it, they don't feel that they've suffered for it at all. But Your Honour, in this particular case, ITN had film of a festival, a pop festival. There was a civil action for damages, and the plaintiff there wanted the outtakes -- in other words, those that weren't seen. And there was then a hearing. And what Lord Denning said about it -- you were quoted part of it. But can I take Your Honours back to the principles, which are on page 33 of the judgement. Your Honour, at page 33 Lord Denning dealt with the principles. Leaving out the first words. "ITN desire guidance as to the circumstances in which they should be required to produce the untransmitted film and show it to the Court. They do not claim an absolute privilege but they draw attention to several matters which may make it undesirable for production to be ordered." And then they -- they pointed to their duty to present news with accuracy and impartiality. And they went on: "Next they say --" and this is -- really goes to the heart of Mr. Robertson's argument on war correspondents -- "if they were to produce untransmitted film, their reporting teams might be exposed to violence more than they are at present. I do not myself see the force of this point. If a crowd of people attack a cameraman, it is because they do not want their actions to appear on the transmitted part of the news and not because of the untransmitted portion." Then they dealt with the point that these items might be misleading. And then goes on to deal with the question of which bits -- how they would identify which were the relevant parts of film, which again doesn't affect us. Then we come to the paragraph that begins: "Next there is the special position of the journalist or reporter who gathers news of public concern. The courts respect his work and will not hamper it more than is necessary. They will seek to achieve a balance between these two matters. On the one hand, there is the public interest which demands that the course of justice should not be impeded by the withholding of evidence. On the other hand, there is the public interest in seeing that confidences are respected and that newsmen are not hampered by fear of being compelled to disclose all the information which comes their way." And they refer to one of the authorities, which is, I think, a footnote in the American authorities to which Your Honours have been referred; that is, the democratic national committee versus McCord. Which I think arose out of the Watergate saga. And then as we said in this court -- and he refers to his own case: "The judge will not direct him, the journalist, to answer unless not only is it relevant but also it is a proper and indeed a necessary question in the course of justice to be put and answered." Then there's the question of the expense, and then this: "In the light of all these considerations, I think that on due notice being given the courts have the power to order the ITN to produce and show the untransmitted film when the course of justice so requires. But the court should exercise this power only when it is likely that the film will have a direct and important place in the determination of the issues before the Court. The mere assertion that the film may have some bearing will not be enough. If the judge considers that the request is irrelevant or fishing or speculative or oppressive, he should refuse it." Your Honour, in other words, it's fairly and squarely within the discretion of the judge to exercise the proper balancing exercise that was referred to by Judge Hunt in his decision between the competing needs, that is, of the ability of journalists to report and to obtain information without the threat of inevitable disclosure coming. Your Honour, that would be the other side of the coin, as it were; in other words, that if a journalist knew that a member of the public or a defendant or the Prosecution had only to ask for a summons, they would have to testify, well, of course that may have an effect. But equally undesirable, as I've already said, is the other extreme side of the coin, a complete blanket immunity. Your Honour, in respect of the American line of authorities, it is our submission -- and I don't go -- propose to go through them, because Your Honours have them and have seen our arguments on this matter -- that the position is very much the same. There is a certain degree of -- and I use the privilege in its loosest proper term as opposed to legal term -- given to journalists in that if they can show that there's a proper reason why the information should not be disclosed, either through an informant or they should not testify for whatever reason, then the courts will grant them that latitude. But in each case, it's a matter for the courts. What about the prospect -- or the aspect, rather, that's raised, and that really that those who report from war areas should have, such as it were, a blanket immunity. Your Honours, we say once you start giving this type of immunity, the courts will find themselves, we would submit, in somewhat of a difficulty. What particular part of the journalist's activities in a war zone is covered by this immunity? Is it Mr. Randal, who sits in Mr. Brdjanin's office in Banja Luka in the municipal building and interviews at that stage a politician? Is it the person, as we've all read about, who was covering action in a country and was wounded, or the journalists who were killed? But the reality is, if one looks at the list of journalists killed -- and no one has any doubt -- and it's not the Prosecution's job for -- at all to suggest that the journalists who brave those sort of conditions, who go into war zones to report what is happening, are brave men fulfilling a public function. But the -- they get killed not on any showing because it is thought that they are going to testify but because they are reporting what the particular side that takes an action does not want them to report. To take a very recent example that's been in the press, no journalists were allowed into the town of Jenin in Israel for a length of time, presumably because nobody wanted them to report what was happening there. But to say that because they go into a war zone they can never be compelled to testify, Your Honour, would, in our submission -- to ignore the reality. And the reality sometimes is that journalists are the only people who are in a position to ensure or to assist the Prosecution of war criminals. If they are the only people who saw a particular action, who went into the camps and filmed what was happening, we submit it would be wrong that the prosecution are people responsible for such crimes could not take place. Your Honour, the overriding international public interest, which is why this Tribunal was established, is that people should be brought for trial for alleged offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think, Ms. Korner, in all fairness to Mr. Robertson's submissions, he does concede to you in paragraph 13 that in the event of the journalist or his testimony is of crucial importance to the determination of a defendant's guilt -- forget innocence for the time being, because that would be more the responsibility of -- of the Court than of the party -- in that case, he definitely is not claiming any qualified privilege. He is conceding that the Court or Tribunal, whatever that would be, would have a right to insist on the journalist giving evidence. So that is conceded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that was very much my impression from listening to Mr. Robertson's argument. But there is still the underlying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... too --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- The underlying theme that journalists should have this privilege, immunity which is theirs and theirs alone to waive. In fact, as one can really see from this case, it's more the -- the employer of the journalist who decides whether or not the journalist will or will not testify, because it's plain from what's been said that it's the Washington Post who stepped in and dealt with this. But Your Honour, I am content -- may I put it this way -- I am content with the principle that the courts of course should be careful and wary about compelling a journalist to disclose his source or to testify, but it is in the end a matter for the courts to rule upon if the Prosecution decide that this is a proper case to issue a witness summons. Your Honours, we do not either quarrel with the code of federal regulations that has been referred to by Mr. Robertson. Obviously in all cases all responsible prosecuting authorities would hesitate before seeking the testimony of people who have been news gathering or going further and compelling them to testify. But Your Honour, we would submit that is -- this is the principle which Your Honours ought to deal with. Your Honours, unless I can assist any further or there's anything else you'd wish me to say on the principle, can I turn, then, to the actual immediate facts of -- I think I must say something about Mr. Randal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Randal, as I've already said, interviewed Mr. Brdjanin in his office and published that interview. There's now some suggestion, although Mr. Randal had never said it -- he said he didn't see him again when he wanted to -- that because of the interview, Mr. Brdjanin refused to see him again. Well, Your Honour, that, of course, is already the point. It's the publication of that interview which has, if anything, caused Mr. Randal -- caused Mr. Brdjanin or others not the talk to journalists. And in each case, Your Honour, if there is a refusal or if journalists are placed in danger, it's because of what they report on and what they publish. And we submit that there is no additional, as it were, danger or shunning if at a later stage the journalist is asked to come to court and confirm that what he published was in fact truthful and accurate. Your Honour, this is not a case -- I'll say it again -- where Mr. Randal is being asked to testify about a confidential source. Your Honour, this is a case where the Prosecution alleges that the media were used by probably all sides -- but as we're dealing with the Bosnian Serbs -- by the Bosnian Serbs for the dissemination of propaganda, Mr. Brdjanin, from the evidence that Your Honour has already heard, was one of the arch proponents of the spreading of that propaganda. Your Honour, this is a case where Mr. Randal made a statement, agreed however reluctantly -- and let me just remind Your Honour of what appears at the bottom of his statement. If I can just find it. "I am willing --" Your Honour, this is the bottom of page 3. "I am willing to speak with the investigators for the Tribunal, but I hesitate as a journalist to testify before the Court. All he's being asked to do is to testify what was said in that article, leaving aside the question that he was using another journalist as a translator. Your Honours, as I said when I began my address to you, it's not perhaps the ideal basis of fact to mount this particular argument of principle, because our submission is there's no merit in the purpose of this application, which is to set this witness summons aside. utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to for the record -- I'm sure I've said all these things to Your Honours and that they're in the record somewhere. X is the person who speaks Serbo-Croatian; Mr. Randal does not. So what we have is a report of that meeting written by someone who could understand the language and a report written by someone who could not. More than that, the report written by Witness X or person X or reporter X provides the background of the basis for the interview in the first place. And it's my position that that background makes the testimony irrelevant and inadmissible. The Prosecutor suggests that it's admissible. Statements made a month and a half after this indictment closes is admissible because it shows a state of mind that existed during the course of the indictment. If one looks at the report of reporter X, it's clear that the purpose of the visit with Mr. Brdjanin as Minister of Housing was to seek his views regarding the Vance Owen proposal that would have made a Serb canton out of the Banja Luka area and to ask him how he leaves as housing minister the business of population relocations would and should occur as a result of that. That was either cut from by the newspaper that published the article of Mr. Randal or he never wrote that part of it in the first place. But it puts his article in a position where it does not reflect the true nature of the interview and the context within which it was given and makes what is irrelevant appear to be relevant. I have agreed that the article written by reporter X can be admitted without that reporter being brought here and without objection by me. And if it's a true report of that interview that the Prosecution seeks, that's the one that should be admitted. But the Prosecution in fact seeks what is an untrue report -- certainly in the sense that it leaves out the context. And so that is my position for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, and I hope to be short. As far as Mr. Ackerman's point is concerned, can I say it is no part of our case to say whether this testimony is irrelevant, slightly relevant, or considerably relevant. That is a matter for the Court. It is of course a matter that you would apply in any balancing act or exercise of judgement as to whether it was necessary for the Prosecution to compel the journalist's testimony. But all I would say is that it -- the fact that the two articles -- one article is longer than the other -- may simply mean that editing was done at Mr. X's newspaper because we all know that journalists file long reports that frequently get cut because of the space requirements of their papers. So the suggestion that it's -- Mr. Randal's report was simply because it was longer or contained material that didn't feature in the other report was therefore untrue is -- has to be illogical. But on the merits of this case, it is -- the fact that remains is that it's accepted by the Prosecution that Mr. Randal gave evidence of what he was told by an interpreter. And it -- I simply refer you -- I think it's in our case, in our motion to the Delalic case, the interpreter case where the Trial Chamber said this, and I quote: "An interpreter cannot be relied upon to testify on the evanescent words of his interpretation in the proceedings between the parties." The most, therefore that, Mr. Randal could give apart from perhaps a comment on the defendant's demeanour and would-be evidence of the evanescent words which had been conveyed to him by Mr. X. One would have the -- the Court would have the unhelpful situation, I suspect, at the end of the day if it compelled Mr. Randal in a position where Mr. X had not been compelled that Mr. Randal would spend much of his time defending Mr. X from Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination, and that would not be perhaps a helpful situation. So that is all I say on the facts apart from this: Ms. Korner said -- and she was speculating -- that Mr. Randal was willing to give evidence until she said the Washington Post stepped in. That is not in fact true. It was and is not a correct speculation. Mr. Randal made clear when he was in a sense -- when the Tribunal investigator arrived at his doorstep, he being in retirement, he made clear that he did not want to testify. He did give a statement, because the investigator was there and he was a great supporter of the Tribunal. But he was unhappy about it. He spoke with his colleagues and he spoke with the newspaper and decided that he definitely did not want to give evidence. And that is -- that is his position. And it -- of course, there not being any case or any clear guidance for journalists, then that is his entitlement. And it's not as though the newspaper has stepped in to stop him, as the Red Cross did. It's an entirely different situation, because the newspaper's own policy respects the rights of conscience of their own journalists to testify or not. And I hope I made clear at the outset that the Washington Post's position was that, as shown by Mr. Jones, was that if its journalists wanted to testify as a matter of their own conscience for either Prosecution or Defence, that was they right, that this test only comes in to stop -- or to limit compulsory process when sought to be exercised against an unwilling journalist. And of course, if the -- one would not want the decision -- Your Honours' decision to turn on the question of whether Mr. Randal was willing at the beginning, because in that event journalists would simply refuse to give statements to investigators. And there may be some situations where journalists can usefully and helpfully give information or statements to investigators without losing their privilege of not testifying. So that is all I would say on the position of Mr. Randal. To come back to the issue of principle, Ms. Korner said repeatedly that we were seeking a blanket immunity. We're seeking no such thing. We are seeking a qualified public interest privilege; alternatively a presumption against forcing a coercive testimony. We do not seek a blanket immunity. We do accept that in exceptional cases, the privilege can be overridden. Now, Ms. Korner's main plank of law were two English cases from which she read. One was Mulholland, and the other was British Steel. I wasn't aware that those cases were going to feature, and therefore perhaps my response to her may be less polite than it otherwise would have been. These cases are dead cases. They are gone from British case law. They represent English common law at a primitive stage of its development. No counsel would cite them today and no counsel does cite them today because they have been overruled firstly by the British parliament, which in 1981 precisely because British Steel and Granada had decided that journalists had no privilege -- decided that journalists must have a privilege and they passed the 1981 Contempt Act to reverse Mulholland and British Steel. And the 1981 Contempt of Court Act will be found in Goodwin at paragraph 20. It gives journalists a qualified privilege to decline to name their sources unless certain very important conditions are met. That is the first way in which Mulholland and British Steel have been consigned to the dustbin of British legal history. The second way is through the European convention. Mulholland was decided in 1963 before Britain had given the right of individual partition in 1966 and the European convention provided, as Goodwin shows, journalists with precisely the right that they were denied in Mulholland and in British Steel. What is most -- what I do protest most vigorously about is the suggestion -- I think it came in Lord Justice Donovan's decision in Mulholland that the journalist should be ordered to testify if he could serve quite "a useful purpose." Article 19 of the international convention on civil political rights and Article 10 and all the jurisprudence under those articles says that the test is whether it is necessary and that questions of usefulness, expediency and the like are nothing to the point. So Mulholland is part of that primitive era of English law where rights were not -- particularly free speech rights and human rights were not acknowledged, as they should have been by English law, which is why England now has a human rights act and incorporates the European convention and so on, and it would be most retrograde and indeed open this Court to critical and visible comment were it to develop a progressive modern rule that was based on these pre-convention -- pre-European convention and pre-contempt of court act authorities which have been decisively rejected in Britain. One can see that by looking at case -- the last case in our bundle, the case of Bright, which was the final -- the most recent case decided on the subject of protecting journalists from compulsory process. And one sees that the -- as is the English reporting convention, that on the second page the cases referred to in the judgements are set out. And just so you can see what was before the Court, the cases referred to in the legal arguments are then set out. And I think it's right to say that in neither section on pages 663 or 664 does one find either Mulholland or British Steel. The reason for that, of course, is that they are not longer of any authority at all on this issue in Britain. But one sees Senior v. Holdsworth and Goodwin, which is X and Morgan-Grampian publishers, referred to as 664, which were cases of course cited before the Court. So we do say that the -- they are far from being classic statements of principle, they are superseded statements of principle which have been rejected within the jurisdiction from which they emanate and that they were -- arose as a result of a law that was found and is regarded now as defective in its protection for journalists, so that the authority on which the Prosecution rely should not be followed. Of course Senior v. Holdsworth has survived from that era because it was a progressive decision which showed that there was -- the judges recognised or were coming to recognise the importance of a public interest privilege for journalists, and that has been now recognised far more as a result of the European convention and the other international law cases that I presented. So that leaves us, I think, with not a great deal between the Prosecutor and the applicant. The Prosecutor says, "Do it as a matter of discretion or consider in your discretion these issues." We say, "No, judicial discretion is a slippery slope. It's a subjective matter which obviously in many situations has to be relied on. But if there's a better solution than discretion, particularly in a criminal case when it should be adopted and that because of the importance of this matter to journalists and because of the importance of journalists to justice in the way that Richard Goldstone explained, we would invite the Court to concretise the -- the situation by making it either a presumption, which means that in -- before exercising the discretion or the discretion is exercised with the starting point, the principles for which we've contended the formula that a journalist ought not to be compelled unless he or she falls within that narrow area of exceptional cases which satisfy the three conditions, or else it be approached as a public interest privilege, the public interest of protecting the journalist in war zones being trunked only when the evidence is -- is necessary, essential, crucial, whatever test the Court chooses to apply, but certainly not merely useful, which would be a dangerous, outmoded, and in fact disregarded test. And so with that, that is really, I think, the -- the choice that faces the Court between the position of the Prosecutor and the position of the applicant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honour's legal officer or secretary contacts us, we -- just to confirm the order, then we can do what we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. On the other hand, the same matter. I'm not quite sure, but the possibility is there. Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau, please do check if there are any of the documents that you made use of during the Banja Luka which may have not been tendered as exhibits. I have a suspicion that there might be. I do have in my file some documents forthcoming from your side in particular -- Mr. Ackerman. Not Madam Fauveau's. I mean, Madam Fauveau's seems to be complete. But your case I seem to have some -- some documents which I don't recall you making use of them during your cross-examinations. But they have certainly not been tendered as exhibits. So please do check that as well so that at least as far as possible I can lock the Banja Luka folders with the documentation for future reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told that we have documents from 1 through 64. We're trying to straighten out now what's been tendered and what hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it may be that the easiest way to solve it is to tender them all -- re-tender them all and -- rather than spend hours trying to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Give us until Monday and we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can -- I'm not putting any deadlines on this. It's something which I'm asking for you cooperation. So it's not a question of putting deadlines. Thank you. So the -- we are adjourned till Monday morning. We'll be meeting in this courtroom. And as agreed, there will be the judge continuing his evidence from where he left it a week -- two weeks ago. I thank you all. And have a nice weekend. Thank you.
